title: AI Is Spending a Trillion Dollars. Physical AI Needs to Show the Return.
summary: AI infrastructure is drawing extraordinary investment. FANUC, Teradyne and a new refinery deployment show where industrial demand is becoming revenue, profit and measurable returns.

AI Is Spending a Trillion Dollars. Physical AI Needs to Show the Return.

29 cents.

That's how much additional gross operating benefit Honeywell estimates its new industrial AI platform could generate for every barrel of oil processed at Nigeria's Dangote refinery.

At full capacity, that could mean more than $60 million in annual benefits from a single facility.

The savings are still projections. But it's an unusually concrete number in an industry where the conversation often revolves around what AI might eventually accomplish.

Now consider the other side of the story.

On Tuesday, Moody's warned that the AI infrastructure boom is creating significant refinancing risks. The ratings agency expects five major U.S. hyperscalers and CoreWeave to spend nearly $1 trillion on capital investments in 2027 alone.

That's an extraordinary amount of money being committed to building intelligence.

And increasingly, the question is what all that intelligence will actually earn.

For Physical AI, this week's developments offered some encouraging answers. But they also revealed why the next 12 months could look very different across the industry.

The robot boom is showing up in unexpected places

FANUC's latest earnings looked excellent.

The Japanese automation giant reported quarterly orders jumping 49% to approximately $1.93 billion.

But look at what customers were ordering.

Factory-automation orders surged 130% to $709 million. Robot orders grew just 12.6% to $654 million.

Both businesses are expanding, but factory automation is growing considerably faster.

The explanation lies partly in semiconductor manufacturing, AI data centers and the advanced machinery needed to produce their components.

The AI infrastructure boom is already generating substantial industrial demand. General-purpose robotics may eventually become a much larger opportunity, but the equipment needed to build that future is selling today.

Teradyne reinforced the point.

Last week, we highlighted its upcoming earnings as an important test of whether growing robotics sales could translate into a profitable business.

Tuesday's results delivered an encouraging milestone.

Robotics revenue grew 28% to $96 million, and management reported that the division had reached profitability.

That's meaningful progress.

But robotics still accounted for only 7.4% of Teradyne's $1.31 billion in quarterly revenue. Semiconductor testing generated $1.07 billion.

The company's financial performance remains overwhelmingly tied to the AI infrastructure boom, even as its robotics business becomes more commercially interesting.

And that's an important distinction when considering where Physical AI's economic value is emerging.

Getting robots into the real world is becoming less theoretical

There was encouraging news beyond the earnings reports.

Universal Robots and Sereact announced that hundreds of robots had shipped in dual-arm systems to European customer sites, handling applications such as sorting returned merchandise.

That's considerably more useful evidence than another carefully rehearsed robot demonstration, even if the companies haven't disclosed the revenue or profitability associated with those installations.

Agility Robotics also reported more than $300 million in committed multi-year orders for Digit 5, although those commitments remain subject to contractual milestones and are not recognized revenue.

Meanwhile, Bedrock Robotics raised $600 million at a $4.1 billion valuation to expand autonomous construction equipment.

Its approach is particularly interesting: adding intelligence to construction machinery that contractors already own.

There's a practical economic argument here.

Replacing an entire fleet of excavators is expensive. Making existing equipment more productive could be a much easier proposition, provided the technology delivers reliable results.

Honeywell is pursuing a similar opportunity in refineries, while NVIDIA continues developing the software and computing infrastructure intended to make intelligent machines easier to train and deploy.

Different industries. Different technologies.

But the pattern is becoming clearer.

We expect applications that improve existing operations or automate well-defined tasks to find commercial traction sooner than highly flexible machines designed to handle almost anything.

The bigger technological ambitions haven't disappeared. They're simply operating on a longer timetable.

Here's where the financial picture gets complicated

The Federal Reserve entered its October meeting with interest rates at 3.75%–4.00%, while September inflation stood at 3.7%.

For an industry that requires substantial spending on hardware, engineering and manufacturing, financing conditions matter.

And this week's financial reports provided a useful reminder.

Chinese automation supplier Inovance grew quarterly revenue 19%. Sounds encouraging.

But its operating cash flow for the first nine months fell 77%, while inventory increased 54% from year-end.

Management attributed much of the increase to production requirements, strategic stocking and receivables.

That may support future growth. But for now, significantly more capital is tied up in the business.

NXP Semiconductors offered a different picture.

Its broader Industrial & IoT division grew 39%, while the company generated $1.21 billion in quarterly non-GAAP free cash flow, equivalent to nearly 32% of revenue.

These aren't directly comparable businesses, but the difference in financial flexibility is hard to ignore.

One company is spending heavily to support expansion. The other is generating enough cash to finance investments while returning capital to shareholders.

In a market increasingly concerned about AI valuations, corporate borrowing and future returns, those distinctions could become more important.

Technological progress doesn't eliminate the cost of financing it.

What we're watching as 2027 approaches

The Black Scarab Physical AI 15 gained 1.75% during the five trading sessions ending October 27, outperforming the S&P 500's 0.13% gain and the Nasdaq Composite's 0.20% advance, based on our tracked benchmark series.

Despite the rebound, the index remained 6.24% below its October 1 launch level. Our index's price returns exclude currency movements.

That short history tells us little about long-term performance. But the underlying developments offer a more useful picture.

Our outlook for the next 6–12 months remains constructive, particularly for industrial applications where customers can demonstrate measurable productivity improvements.

AI infrastructure spending should continue supporting demand for precision manufacturing, testing equipment and industrial controls. Specialized autonomous systems could also see broader adoption as customers move beyond initial deployments.

General-purpose robotics remains a more uncertain proposition. The technology is advancing, but reliability, integration costs and deployment economics still have considerable room to improve.

And there's an obvious risk to this outlook.

If industrial orders slow, customer pilots fail to convert into repeat purchases, or inventory and financing requirements keep rising faster than cash generation, the commercial transition could take longer than current expectations suggest.

Those are the numbers we'll be watching.

The bottom line

The enormous investment in AI infrastructure is creating real opportunities across the industrial economy. This week's results made that increasingly difficult to dispute.

But the economic rewards aren't arriving everywhere at once.

Some companies are already generating substantial profits supplying the infrastructure boom. Others are beginning to demonstrate profitable robotics operations. More ambitious autonomous systems are attracting enormous investment while their long-term economics remain largely unproven.

We expect all three groups to play important roles in Physical AI's development.

They just aren't likely to reward shareholders on the same timetable.

The next 12 months should provide better evidence of which applications can scale, which suppliers can protect their margins and how much value customers actually receive.

Honeywell's 29 cents per barrel is still only an estimate.

But if those savings start showing up in customers' operating results, they'll tell us something far more important than another impressive robot demonstration.

They'll tell us what Physical AI is worth.
